Let’s dive into Chapter 2: Building a Strategic Foundation—Situational Awareness and Clear Objectives.
Every solid strategy starts with really understanding the situation you’re in. In the military, they call this situational awareness. It’s all about being able to see, understand, and even predict what’s happening around you.
But it’s not just for the battlefield. In business, situational awareness means you’re always gathering info about your market, your competitors, what your team can do, and what’s changing out there in the world. And here’s the thing—this isn’t just a one-and-done task. The environment can shift fast, and new opportunities or threats might pop up when you least expect it.
So, how do teams build this kind of awareness? Well, one classic approach comes from the military world: the SWOT analysis. You might’ve heard of it—it stands for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats. It’s a simple framework, but it packs a punch because it helps you step back and really look at where you stand:
Strengths—what do you already have that gives you an edge?
Weaknesses—where are the gaps, or where could you be vulnerable?
Opportunities—what trends or openings could you take advantage of?
And Threats—what’s out there that could trip you up or steal your market share?
By mapping these out, leaders can avoid nasty surprises and make smarter decisions. Plus, it gets everyone on the same page—no more working off different assumptions or facts.
Now, once you’ve got a solid grip on your environment, the next step is setting clear objectives. In the military, they call it the commander’s intent. It’s a short, powerful statement about what success looks like and why it matters. In business, clear objectives give your team direction and focus—they help everyone prioritize, stay on track, and actually measure whether you’re moving forward.
And here’s a tip: your objectives should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. That way, everyone knows exactly what’s expected—and how you’ll know if you’ve hit the mark.
But watch out for a common trap: trying to do too much at once. It’s tempting to chase every shiny goal, but spreading yourself thin usually leads to confusion and wasted effort. The best leaders pick a handful of critical objectives and put their energy where it counts most.
Here’s something to think about—situational awareness and clear objectives are tightly linked. If you don’t really understand what’s happening around you, your goals might be way off target. But if you don’t have clear objectives, even the best info won’t help, because you won’t know what you’re aiming for.
Let’s make this real with a quick story. Imagine a company gets hit by a sudden market shake-up—maybe a new competitor comes in with a lower-priced product. The leadership team runs a SWOT analysis. They realize their big strength is top-notch customer service, but they’re slow at rolling out new products. The opportunity? Differentiate by offering even better support. The threat? Losing customers who care more about price.
With this in mind, they set a clear objective: launch a new service package in three months, using their customer service advantage to keep current clients and attract folks who value support over a bargain price.
That’s how situational awareness and clear objectives work hand in hand. By always scanning what’s happening and updating your goals, you give your organization the best shot at staying ahead and responding to whatever comes your way.
